title: Resting-State Functional Brain Connectivity and Neurodevelopmental Profile in 3-Year-Olds with Congenital Heart Disease
content: Background/Objectives: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is associated with altered brain development and an increased risk of neurodevelopmental difficulties, particularly in more severe forms of the condition. Although alterations in functional brain connectivity have been reported before and after the first corrective surgery in early infancy, as well as in adulthood, little is known about their presentation in early childhood and their association with neurodevelopmental outcomes. This study aimed to characterize resting-state functional connectivity in 3-year-old children with moderate-to-severe CHD and to examine its associations with neurodevelopmental outcomes, including cognitive, language, and motor abilities. Methods: Twenty-five 3-year-old children with moderate-to-severe CHD and 28 age-matched healthy controls completed resting-state functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and a standardized neurodevelopmental assessment. Functional brain connectivity was examined across frontal, fronto-parietal, left and right fronto-temporal, and inter-hemispheric networks. Group differences were analyzed using ANCOVAs controlling for socioeconomic status (maternal SES) and with sex as a factor. Associations between functional brain connectivity and neurodevelopmental measures were examined using hierarchical linear regression models adjusted for diagnostic group, sex, and socioeconomic status, with connectivity-by-group interactions tested to assess group differences in these associations. Results: Children with moderate-to-severe CHD showed overall lower resting-state functional connectivity and poorer language performance than controls. Greater interhemispheric functional connectivity was associated with fewer executive function difficulties across participants, with no significant differences in these associations between groups. Conclusions: Preschool-aged children with CHD show altered functional connectivity and language vulnerabilities, while the association between interhemispheric connectivity and executive functioning appears to extend across both CHD and typically developing children.
